Testimony of the Office of Child and Family Services
Maine Department of Health and Human Services
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
In support of LD 2001, An Act to Clarifi� the Laws Governing Facilitiesfor Children and Adults
Under the Health and Human Services Laws
Sponsor: Senator Ingwersen Hearing Date: January 14, 2026
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Health and Human Services. My name is Bobbi Johnson, and I serve as the Director of the
Office of Child and Family Services (OCFS) in the Maine Department of Health and Human Services and I am here today to testify in support of LD 2001, An Act to Clarifil the Laws Governing Facilities for Children and Adults Under the Health and Human Services Laws.
This bill is intended to update statutes related to the licensing of facilities for children. This bill
was brought forward by the Department to address inconsistencies related to licensing that are having a negative impact on the Depaitment's Children's Licensing and Investigation Services (CLIS) Team, licensed providers, or both. It includes five components:
Section I of the bill addresses an issue identified for OCFS by OAG that the language of 22 MRSA �7703 makes the records of an investigation of neglect or abuse by the CLIS team
confidential but does not extend that confidentiality beyond the investigation if a finding made
by the team is administratively appealed by the provider. OCFS does not believe that it was the
intent for confidentiality to be limited to the investigation only and not extend to activities during
the administrative review.
Section 2 of the bill corrects an oversight in the work done by OCFS and the Legislature in 2023 when An Act Regarding Investigations of Out-of-home Child Abuse and Neglect (PL 2023, c.
248) was enacted and relocated the statutes for investigation of out-of-home child abuse and neglect to the Child and Family Services and Child Protection Act. Thus, this change provides the confidentiality of both provider and client information throughout any proceedings that might
follow the finding.
Section 3 of the bill corrects a recently identified issue with changes enacted in 2019 in An Act to Increase the Availability of Foster Homes (PL 2019, c. 444). That bill sought to eliminate the
requirement that resource (also known as foster) homes be subject to a State Fire Marshal
inspection. It was OCFS' intent at the time that the exception to this requirement would extend to
all resource homes, but it has become clear that there is more specificity needed to the language
of the statute in order to appropriately effectuate that intent.

Section 4 of the bill removes an outdated reference to a statutory requirement for interagency
licensing that no longer occurs between DHHS and DOE because each entity conducts their own
independent licensing and approval process for any providers that cross-over into the authority of both Departments, ensuring equity for all providers and safety for children regardless of the
setting.
Section 5 of the bill removes another outdated reference, this time to a licensing requirement specific only to child care providers licensed as nursery schools, that requires they provide a declaration from a licensed medical provider at least every two years that certifies that the
administrator or another staff member of the nursery school is "free from communicable
disease" . This requirement is not present in the license statute for any other type of licensed child care provider, which results in an undue burden to just one type of licensed child care provider.
OCFS is asking for your support in addressing these issues to best streamline the operations for our talented and dedicated CLIS team, as well as for child welfare as OCFS seeks the continued
removal of barriers to licensing as a resource home just as was intended by the 2019 bill.
Thank you for your time and attention. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have and to make myself available for questions at the work session.

Dear Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
Thank you for the opportunity to submit written testimony regarding LD 2001.
Although this bill is framed as technical clarification, it makes substantive changes that concern me deeply. As
written, LD 2001 centralizes authority within DHHS, reduces external oversight, limits transparency, and weakens routine inspection requirements. Taken together, these changes increase risk to children rather than improving safety or accountability.
I want to be clear that I support protecting personal privacy in abuse and neglect cases. However, process
failures and decision-making rationale are not private information. They are government actions. When
children are seriously harmed or die, the public and Legislature must be able to understand what decisions were made, why they were made, and where systems failed. Transparency does not require disclosure of identities. It requires disclosure of system performance. Without that, accountability is impossible.
I am also concerned about consolidating licensing and investigative functions within DHHS. Centralizing licensing, enforcement, investigations, and rulemaking under one agency increases the risk that DHHS is effectively investigating itself. DHHS is already stretched thin, and consolidation without significant staffing
investment increases burnout and turnover, which directly undermines safety and consistency.
The removal of routine inspections for family foster homes and specialized children's homes is particularly troubling. These homes serve high-risk children, and conditions can and do change over time. Routine inspections are not punitive. They are preventative. Eliminating them assumes safety remains static after
placement, which is not realistic and puts children at risk.
I also oppose eliminating interagency licensing. Redundancy in child safety systems is not waste; it is protection. Shared oversight provides checks and balances that prevent blind spots and ensure accountability when systems fail.
l am not suggesting that DHHS be removed from child welfare, foster care, or abuse and neglect investigations. lam suggesting that licensing authority for day care and early childhood programs and centers
be transferred to the Department of Education. Day care programs are early childhood education settings governed by developmental expectations, programming standards, and school readiness outcomes. Licensing
these programs through DOE would better align oversight with educational programming, support implementation of LD 345, and allow DHHS to focus its limited capacity on higher~risk child welfare functions. DHHS would retain authority over health, safety, and abuse response, with mandatory cross-reporting
between agencies.
1

While the communicable disease clearance requirement for nursery school staff is reasonable, it does not offset the broader concerns outlined above. For these reasons, I oppose LD 2001 as written and urge the Committee to reject provisions that reduce transparency, eliminate routine inspections, and remove interagency oversight. Children need visible systems, shared accountability, and public trust -- not streamlined bureaucracy. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Respectfully,
Colleen Brown, M.Ed. Whiting, Maine 207-263-6047 Email: 207puffinpines@gmait.oom

Testimony ofSenator Henry Ingwersen introducing
LD 2001, An Act to Clarify the Laws Governing Facilities for Children and Adults Under the Health and Human Services Laws
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
Wednesday, January 14, 2026
Representative Meyer, and fellow Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and
Human Services. As you know, I am Senator Henry Ingwersen, representing Senate District 32,
which includes Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman. I am here to present LD 2001, "An Act to Clarify the Laws Governing Facilities for Children and Adults under the Health and Human Services Laws."
I have sponsored this bill on behalf of the Office of Child and Family Services, an office within
the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) that we are all familiar with. In
discussion with the Department, I understand that they have identified a few areas of statute relating to the laws governing the licensing of facilities for children that need to be changed or updated. This bill will do that through five specific changes, which I will allow the Department
to detail, following my testimony.
In short, this legislation would address a confidentiality issue, correct a statutory reference
regarding the consolidations of functions, clarify licensing requirements under 22 MRSA �8l03,
remove statutory reference to collaboration between DHHS and the Department of Education
(DOE) that no longer occurs, and eliminate a burdensome requirement that was applied only to
child care providers licensed as nursery school programs.
I hope that you will join me in supporting this effort to provide statutory clarity for OCFS and for
those their licensing requirements impact. I ask that you hold any questions you may have for the
Department.
Thank you.

Henry Ingwersen
State Senator, Senate District 32
Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman
